anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction patterns are written so that they process far more rows, data, or time than business logic actually requires.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions request incompatible locks on the same resources, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that stall progress until a victim is rolled back.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes collectively drive host CPU utilization to saturation, starving runnable tasks of compute cycles.

When these three root causes surface together, the database experiences prolonged statement runtimes, widespread blocking and deadlock storms, and system-wide latency spikes amplified by CPU exhaustion. Slow or looping SQL generated by the application touches excessive rows; each over-sized operation acquires larger and longer-held locks, expanding the duration and scope of lock queues. As blocked sessions spin on the scheduler or are repeatedly aborted and retried by the application, runnable threads accumulate, driving host CPU to sustained 90-100 % utilization. High CPU, in turn, lengthens context-switch and lock acquisition times, so even moderately contended resources become severe choke points. Monitoring views show simultaneous surges in slow-query counts, lock-wait time, deadlock reports, and CPU run-queue depth; application layers observe timeouts, cascading retries, and throughput collapse.

Causal chain: inefficient SQL patterns (wide scans, large batches, open-ended transactions) dramatically increase the number of rows touched and the lifetime of locks. The enlarged lock footprint raises the probability and duration of conflicting lock requests, producing blocking trees and deadlocks. Blocked or killed transactions are commonly retried by application logic, further inflating concurrency pressure. Meanwhile each bloated statement consumes more CPU per execution; the retries, lock-manager housekeeping, and victim rollbacks add still more CPU load. CPU saturation slows down every thread, including those that could otherwise release locks quickly, thereby feeding a feedback loop: prolonged execution keeps locks held, extended locks intensify contention, contention causes retries, and retries plus heavy scanning drive CPU to its limits. The intertwined effects of inefficient workload design, lock contention, and compute starvation thus reinforce one another, creating a severe performance degradation scenario typical of high-throughput OLTP systems.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
